notes.1: This question required candidates to recognise that the boiling point would be higher than the melting point and that pure substances tend to have sharp melting and boiling points rather than a range of values. All of the distractors were chosen with Distractor B being the most common.
notes.2: Few candidates chose Distractor A or Distractor B . Weaker candidates were more likely to choose Distractor C , the diagram which represents a single compound only.
notes.3: This question was not well answered. Many candidates appeared to confuse the number of electrons in the outer shell with the number of electron shells and chose Distractor C .
notes.4: This question discriminated well between the most and least able candidates, with many appearing to be guessing. All the distractors were equally chosen by the least able candidates.
notes.5: The more able candidates had little difficulty with this question whereas none of the less able candidates answered this question correctly. Distractor B was the most common incorrect answer. Candidates are reminded that solid metals react by losing electrons to become cations.
notes.6: This question discriminated well between the most and least able candidates. Distractor C was the most common incorrect answer.
notes.7: Over half of the candidates chose Distractor C . Iron( III ) oxide is an ionic substance and argon is monatomic so only methane and chlorine contain covalent (electron sharing) bonds.
notes.9: An equal number of candidates chose the correct answer and Distractor D . More than one in seven candidates chose Distractor A which has both an incorrect symbol for cobalt and an incorrect ratio of cation to anion.
notes.10: This question required careful reading to identify the correct answer. Relative masses are always given on the atomic scale and so all options which do not reference an atom (or one atom) must be incorrect. The relative atomic mass is calculated from an average of the isotopes to give a single value.
notes.14: Few candidates chose Distractor B or Distractor D and so correctly identified the link between temperature and energy change. Distractor A was chosen by the majority of candidates showing a common confusion in this representation of exothermic and endothermic reactions.
notes.16: During a chemical reaction, if a substance is oxidised or reduced it must be one of the reactants on the left - hand side of the reaction arrow. A quarter of the candidates chose Distractor B or Distractor C , which are both reaction products.
notes.17: Overall the distribution of answers suggests that many candidates were guessing. Many candidates find the recall of indicator colours difficult.
notes.18: The correct answer was the least popular choice for this question. At this level candidates are required to know that redox reactions involve the gain or loss of oxygen. Reaction 1 was combustion which requires oxygen and reaction 2 was rusting which requi res both water and oxygen.
notes.19: Across all the candidates the four options were equally chosen. Weaker candidates favoured Distractor A but the only non - metal oxide present was carbon dioxide.
notes.21: Four out of five of the weaker candidates chose Distractor B or Distractor C which both describe an increase in metallic character. Candidates are advised to use the Periodic Table provided to check their answer by referring to the position of elements they know well such as iron or oxygen.
notes.22: Although the stronger candidates tended to choose the correct answer more than any other option, weaker candidates tended to choose Distractor C showing recall of the trend in reactivity of Group I elements but not their physical properties.
notes.24: Weaker candidates appeared to be guessing with all the options frequently chosen. More able candidates had little problem with this question.
notes.25: This question was not well answered. Many candidates did not recall or check that helium only has two outer shell electrons. Statement 1 is therefore incorrect. Most candidates chose Distractor B .
notes.26: Across all candidates all the options were commonly chosen with a preference for Distractor C by the less able candidates and Distractor A by the more able. It could help candidates to remember the order of reactivity of the elements by using a mnemonic generator. The more reactive elements such as aluminium are more difficult to extract from their ores and require electrolysis rather than s imple reduction using carbon or carbon monoxide.
notes.27: This question was not well answered. Almost half of the candidates chose Distractor A . Although statement 2 is a correct statement it does not answer the question to explain why aluminium is used in place of copper for power cables. It would explain the reverse argument.
notes.29: The four options were equally chosen by the weaker candidates, whereas the stronger candidates overall had little difficulty with this question.
notes.30: This was a challenging question and fewer than a third of the candidates answered correctly. Candidates were required to recall that clean, dry air is 21 per cent oxygen and that oxygen reacts readily, when heated with copper. Many candidates assumed no reaction would occur and chose Distractor D .
notes.31: Distractor A was chosen by more than third of the candidates overall. In common with the theory papers, candidates often confuse the origin and adverse effects of common air pollutants.
notes.34: The majority of candidates assumed that ‘compound Z ’ was an alkene. The formula given matches C H n 2n+2 and so Z is an alkane. The syllabus describes alkanes as only reacting in combustion or in substitution reactions with chlorine which gives the answer. Distractor C was chosen by over a third of the candidates overall.
notes.35: All four options were equally chosen by candidates. Candidates should recall that alcohol compounds contain the – OH group and carboxylic acid contain the – COOH group which will help in eliminating the options in this question.
notes.36: Candidates are advised to use a mnemonic generator to devise a method to recall the order of the petroleum fractions. Most candidates suggested Distractor B , reversing the order of gasoline and naphtha fractions.
notes.37: Most candidates identified ethene as a hydrocarbon but confused the meaning of saturated and unsaturated. Distractor B was the most popular choice. Most candidates knew that ethene is reactive and so Distractor D was chosen by few candidates.
notes.38: The precision of measuring apparatus is not well known by some candidates. A 25 cm measuring cylinder would measure to the nearest 1 cm and so 25.0 or 25.5 could be recorded. Only the burette could be used to measure to two decimal places.
notes.40: Although most candidates correctly identified the colour produced by sodium ions in a flame test, many candidates did not recognise that effervescence after the addition of a dilute acid indicated either a pure metal or a carbonate compound. Distractor A was the most common answer.
notes.general_comments: Candidates found this to be an accessible paper overall with many questions showing good discrimination between candidates. A good spread of marks was seen although fewer candidates scored the higher marks. Overall candidates found Question 1 , 3 , 8 , 21 and 25 to have the least challenge.
